newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH YIELDS SEEN RISING, ZLOTY OUTLOOK MIXED.
newsitem.headline: POLISH YIELDS SEEN RISING, ZLOTY OUTLOOK MIXED.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields are seen extending a nearly two-month growth trend at next Monday's primary tender but analyst expectations on the zloty's moves next week were mixed on Friday.
Analysts said demand would fall short or roughly match the treasury's 900 million zloty offer and that minimum prices would fall by one or two groszes for all maturities.

"Yields should continue to rise in December as inflation expectations are high...and corporates start focusing on closing annual accounts, not on purchasing paper," said Dariusz Kaliszuk, T-bill dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.
Analysts expected the average yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill to inch up toward 19.60 percent from 19.54 this week and the average yield of the 26-week paper to 19.25 from 19.23 percent.
The 13-week T-bill average yield was seen rising to around 18.78 percent from 18.73 as corporate demand for paper cools during the last month of the year.
On Monday the treasury offers 600 million zlotys of the benchmark, 300 million of 26-week T-bills and 200 million of 13-week paper.

Analysts played down this week's statements by a deputy president of the the National Bank of Poland (NBP), who signalled that the central bank may consider raising interest rates in 1997 to curb fast growing demand.
"Rates are not likely to rise, if anything the NBP will rather leave them alone for some time," said Wojciech Labryga, T-bill dealer at Bank Slaski SA.

Next week's scenario seemed less clear for the zloty, which climbed to a monthly high of nearly 2.3 percent below the trading band centre on Wednesday only to fall back to around 2.1 percent by the end of the week.
Analysts said the mid-week surge amid a short-lived cash shortage on the money market pulled up the zloty to levels attractive for foreign investors to sell Polish T-bills.

Some analysts expected the zloty to fall below two percent from parity early next week and possibly test 1.7 percent as importers' orders and a deteriorating current account push the currency downward.
Others said privatisation or foreign direct investment inflows would buoy the zloty next week or at least keep it from losing ground against the basket of five western currencies.
The zloty closed the week at 2.8485 to the dollar and 1.8560 to the mark, or about 2.13 percent from the parity rate.

One-day deposit rates were expected to coast along around the 14-day drainage rate of 19.16 percent next week as no large cash inflows were likely to stir up liquidity in the first week of December monthly reserve period.
"I do not expect the central bank to intervenue on the money market next week as there are no surpluses to drain," said Alicja Wolanska from Raiffeisen Centrobank in Warsaw.
